document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman attends her first prenatal visit at 12 weeks gestation. Her obstetrical history includes a son delivered vaginally at 39 weeks, a daughter delivered at 33 weeks, a spontaneous miscarriage at 9 weeks, and an ectopic pregnancy managed with methotrexate. Both children are alive and well. Which of the following best describes her obstetrical history in GTPAL format?
questions.explanation: Gravidity is the total number of pregnancies of any gestation and includes the current pregnancy, abortions, ectopic pregnancies, and molar pregnancies, giving G5 here. Term deliveries are those beyond 37 weeks (T1), preterm deliveries are 20+0 to 36+6 weeks (P1), abortions include both miscarriages and ectopic pregnancies ending before 20 weeks (A2), and L is the number of living children (L2).

optionExplanations.a: Omits the current pregnancy from gravidity and counts only one pregnancy loss, whereas both the miscarriage and the ectopic count as abortions.
optionExplanations.b: Gravidity must include the current pregnancy, so the total is five, not four.
optionExplanations.d: The 33-week delivery is preterm (20+0 to 36+6 weeks), not term, so T is 1 and P is 1.
optionExplanations.e: Ectopic pregnancies ending before 20 weeks are counted in the abortion category, so A is 2, not 1.

source.reference: OB3 — Diagnosis of Pregnancy: History (GTPAL)

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman presents for her first prenatal visit. She has regular 28-day menstrual cycles, has not used hormonal contraception, and is certain that the first day of her last menstrual period was 10 May 2025. A dating ultrasound has not yet been arranged. Using Naegele's rule, which of the following is her estimated date of delivery?
questions.explanation: Naegele's rule calculates the estimated date of delivery as the first day of the last menstrual period plus one year, plus seven days, minus three months, with adjustment when the cycle length differs from 28 days. Applying this to 10 May 2025 gives 10 May 2026, then 17 May 2026, then 17 February 2026. Her cycles are 28 days, so no correction is needed.

optionExplanations.a: This subtracts a full three months without adding the seven days required by the rule, and then over-corrects.
optionExplanations.b: This omits the addition of seven days to the last menstrual period date.
optionExplanations.d: This adds fourteen rather than seven days to the last menstrual period date.
optionExplanations.e: This subtracts only two months instead of three.

source.reference: OB4 — Initial Prenatal Visit: History (Naegele's Rule)

questions.question: A 26-year-old primigravida at 9 weeks gestation reports nausea and several episodes of vomiting daily. She remains well hydrated, her weight is stable, and urine ketones are negative. Frequent small bland meals, ginger, extra rest, and stopping her iron-containing prenatal vitamin have not relieved her symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological therapy?
questions.explanation: For nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, first-line pharmacological therapy is pyridoxine (vitamin B6) monotherapy or the doxylamine/pyridoxine combination, dosed as 4 tablets orally daily up to a maximum of 8 tablets per day. This patient has already tried the recommended non-pharmacological measures without success and has no features of dehydration or ketosis.

optionExplanations.a: Ondansetron is reserved for severe nausea and vomiting after other anti-emetics have failed.
optionExplanations.b: Metoclopramide is used as adjunctive therapy for severe nausea and vomiting, not as first-line treatment.
optionExplanations.d: Phenothiazines such as prochlorperazine are adjunctive agents for severe symptoms rather than initial therapy.
optionExplanations.e: Acid-reducing medications are adjunctive therapy and do not treat the nausea and vomiting directly.

source.reference: OB5 — Nausea and Vomiting: Management

questions.question: A healthy 30-year-old woman and her partner, both of Ashkenazi Jewish descent, attend a preconception counselling visit. Neither has a personal or family history of genetic disease, and both have normal complete blood counts. Their physician discusses ancestry-based carrier screening and wishes to screen the couple for Tay-Sachs disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test?

options.text: Mean corpuscular volume and mean corpuscular hemoglobin on CBC

questions.explanation: Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive condition for which individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish, French Canadian, and Cajun ancestry are screened. The recommended screening test is a hexosaminidase A enzyme assay or DNA analysis of the HEXA gene. If both partners are positive, referral for genetic counselling is indicated.

optionExplanations.a: Hemoglobin electrophoresis screens for thalassemia and sickle cell disease in at-risk ancestral groups, not Tay-Sachs.
optionExplanations.b: CFTR gene analysis is the screening test for cystic fibrosis, indicated with a family history of cystic fibrosis or a linked condition.
optionExplanations.d: FMR-1 DNA analysis screens for Fragile X syndrome and is indicated with a confirmed or suspected family history.
optionExplanations.e: Red cell indices are used as an initial screen for thalassemia and hemoglobinopathies, and are normal here.

questions.topic: Prenatal Screening: High-Risk Population Carrier Testing

source.reference: OB7 — Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Tests, Table 2

questions.question: A 29-year-old G1 books late and is seen for her first prenatal visit at 17 weeks gestation, confirmed by ultrasound the same day. She is otherwise healthy with no risk factors for aneuploidy and no family history of genetic disease. After counselling, she requests screening for Down syndrome and for open neural tube defects. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening investigation?
questions.explanation: Maternal serum screening is performed at 15-20 weeks gestation and is offered to patients who have missed the window for the enhanced first trimester screen. It measures MSAFP, beta-hCG, unconjugated estriol, and inhibin A, providing risk estimates for trisomy 21 and trisomy 18 as well as screening for open neural tube defects through the MSAFP.

optionExplanations.a: The enhanced first trimester screen is performed at 11-14 weeks and this window has passed.
optionExplanations.b: Nuchal translucency is measured at 11-13+3 weeks and does not screen for open neural tube defects.
optionExplanations.d: Chorionic villus sampling is a diagnostic test performed at 10-12 weeks and does not screen for open neural tube defects.
optionExplanations.e: Amniocentesis is a diagnostic rather than a screening test and is not first-line in a low-risk patient.

source.reference: OB8 — Table 4: Comparison of FTS, MSS, and NIPT

questions.question: A 26-year-old G2P1 with an uncomplicated pregnancy is seen for a routine visit at 28 weeks gestation. Her blood group is O negative and her antibody screen at the first prenatal visit was negative. She has had no bleeding, no trauma, and no invasive procedures during this pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management at this visit?

options.text: Withhold Rh immune globulin until after delivery of an Rh-positive infant
Repeat the antibody screen monthly and treat only if it becomes positive
Perform a Kleihauer-Betke test and treat only if it is positive

questions.explanation: Rh immune globulin is given to all Rh-negative, antibody screen negative patients routinely at 28 weeks gestation, where it provides protection for roughly 12 weeks. It is also given within 72 hours of the birth of an Rh-positive fetus, with invasive procedures, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage or therapeutic abortion, antepartum hemorrhage, and trauma.

optionExplanations.b: Postpartum administration alone omits the routine antenatal dose that prevents sensitization during the third trimester.
optionExplanations.c: Serial monthly antibody titres are used for patients who are already sensitized; prophylaxis is the goal in an unsensitized patient.
optionExplanations.d: The Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage to determine whether additional Rh immune globulin is needed, not whether the routine dose should be given.
optionExplanations.e: The recommended timing of routine antenatal prophylaxis is 28 weeks, not 36 weeks.

source.reference: OB9 — Isoimmunization Screening: Prophylaxis

questions.question: A 30-year-old G2P1 at 34 weeks gestation presents to labour and delivery triage reporting reduced fetal movement for one day. A non-stress test is started. Over the first 20 minutes the baseline is 140 bpm with moderate variability and no decelerations, but there are no accelerations and the patient reports feeling no movement. Which of the following is the next best step?

options.text: Apply vibroacoustic stimulation and continue monitoring for a further 30 minutes
Discharge her with instructions to perform fetal movement counts
Begin an oxytocin infusion for a contraction stress test
Administer betamethasone and repeat the tracing in 24 hours

questions.explanation: A normal non-stress test after 32 weeks requires at least two accelerations of at least 15 bpm above baseline lasting at least 15 seconds within 20 minutes, and a tracing is only called abnormal when there are fewer than two accelerations over 40 minutes. If no accelerations or fetal movements are observed in the first 20 minutes, the fetus should be stimulated with fundal pressure or acoustic/vibratory stimulation and monitoring continued for 30 minutes.

optionExplanations.b: Discharge is inappropriate before the test has been completed and interpreted over the full monitoring period.
optionExplanations.c: An incomplete non-stress test with moderate variability and no decelerations does not indicate immediate operative delivery.
optionExplanations.d: A contraction stress test is not the recommended immediate response to an absence of accelerations in the first 20 minutes.
optionExplanations.e: Corticosteroids address fetal lung maturity and do not resolve the incomplete assessment of fetal well-being.

source.reference: OB10 — Fetal Surveillance: Non-Stress Test, Interpretation

questions.question: A 36-year-old G2P1 at 36 weeks gestation is assessed for decreased fetal movement. A biophysical profile is performed and scores 6/10, with a normal amniotic fluid volume. She has no contractions, bleeding, or leaking of fluid, her vital signs are normal, and the pregnancy has otherwise been uncomplicated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the biophysical profile in 24 hours
Repeat the biophysical profile in one week
Discharge with weekly non-stress tests only

questions.explanation: A biophysical profile of 6/10 with normal amniotic fluid is an equivocal test with variable perinatal mortality, and the recommended action is to repeat the biophysical profile in 24 hours. Scores of 8/10 with normal fluid or 10/10 are reassuring, while 0-4/10 should prompt consideration of delivery for fetal indications.

optionExplanations.b: A one-week interval is far too long for an equivocal score that requires reassessment within 24 hours.
optionExplanations.c: Immediate operative delivery is reserved for scores of 0-4/10 or other evidence of fetal compromise.
optionExplanations.d: Delivery is the response to a 6-8/10 score with abnormal fluid at term, but this patient has normal fluid and an equivocal result.
optionExplanations.e: Discharge without repeating the equivocal biophysical profile does not address the possibility of fetal compromise.

source.reference: OB11 — Biophysical Profile: Interpretation

questions.question: A 30-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks gestation presents with sudden, constant lower back and abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding. Her uterus is tender and firm with no relaxation between frequent contractions. Blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg and heart rate is 122 bpm, which appears out of proportion to the modest amount of visible blood loss. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Preterm labour with a bloody show

questions.explanation: Placental abruption is premature partial or total placental detachment caused by bleeding at the decidual-placental interface after 20 weeks. It typically presents with painful vaginal bleeding of sudden onset localized to the lower back and uterus, uterine tenderness and hypertonus with lack of relaxation between contractions, and shock or anemia out of proportion to the apparent blood loss because bleeding may be concealed.

optionExplanations.a: Placenta previa causes painless bleeding without uterine tenderness or hypertonus.
optionExplanations.c: Vasa previa causes painless bleeding at rupture of membranes with fetal distress from fetal exsanguination, not maternal shock.
optionExplanations.d: Uterine rupture is associated with a previous uterine scar or excessive uterine stimulation, neither described here.
optionExplanations.e: Bloody show is a small amount of blood-stained mucus and does not cause maternal hypotension or a tense, tender uterus.

source.reference: OB15 — Placental Abruption: Clinical Features

questions.question: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 36 weeks gestation has spontaneous rupture of membranes at home, immediately followed by painless bright red vaginal bleeding. On arrival, the fetal heart tracing shows a sinusoidal pattern with bradycardia. A third trimester ultrasound had documented a velamentous cord insertion with unprotected fetal vessels crossing the internal cervical os. Which of the following is the best management?

options.text: Perform an Apt test on the vaginal blood before deciding on delivery
Augment labour with oxytocin to expedite vaginal delivery
Transfuse the mother and manage expectantly until 37 weeks

questions.explanation: In vasa previa the bleeding is fetal in origin, so even a small volume of blood loss can be catastrophic; perinatal mortality is 50% if undiagnosed and rises to 75% once membranes rupture. Management is planned caesarean delivery at 35-36 weeks, or emergency caesarean delivery if bleeding occurs, as it has here with an accompanying sinusoidal tracing and bradycardia.

optionExplanations.b: The Apt test distinguishes fetal from maternal blood but must not delay delivery when the diagnosis is already established and the fetus is compromised.
optionExplanations.c: Continuing labour allows ongoing fetal exsanguination through the exposed vessels.
optionExplanations.d: Maternal transfusion does not address bleeding that is coming from the fetal circulation.
optionExplanations.e: Tocolysis and steroids prolong the pregnancy and are inappropriate once the fetal vessels have ruptured and the fetus is compromised.

source.reference: OB16 — Vasa Previa: Clinical Features and Management

questions.question: A 28-year-old G2P1 whose first child was delivered at term is asymptomatic at 21 weeks gestation. A transvaginal ultrasound performed to check placental location incidentally shows a cervical length of 20 mm. She has no contractions, bleeding, or leaking of fluid, and no history of cervical surgery or spontaneous preterm birth. Which of the following is the best management?

options.text: Vaginal progesterone 200 mg once daily until 36 weeks
Strict bed rest with weekly cervical length measurement
Betamethasone 12 mg IM for two doses

questions.explanation: Progesterone is indicated when the cervical length is less than 25 mm before 24 weeks gestation, given as 200 mg vaginally once daily from the time of diagnosis until 36 weeks. It is superior to cerclage for preventing preterm labour in singleton pregnancies that are not due to cervical incompetence, which is the situation here given the absence of prior preterm birth or cervical procedures.

optionExplanations.b: Cerclage is indicated for cervical incompetence and is considered for a short cervix in women with a prior spontaneous preterm birth, which this patient does not have.
optionExplanations.c: Bed rest alone is not an evidence-based intervention for a short cervix.
optionExplanations.d: Tocolysis is used to suppress established preterm labour, and this patient has no contractions.
optionExplanations.e: Antenatal corticosteroids are given when delivery is expected within seven days, which is not the case for an asymptomatic patient.

source.reference: OB17 — Prevention of Preterm Labour: Progesterone

questions.question: A 27-year-old G1 at 30+2 weeks gestation is admitted in preterm labour with regular painful contractions and a cervix dilated to 6 cm. Membranes are intact and the fetal heart tracing is normal. The obstetrical team judges that delivery is imminent. She received her first dose of betamethasone two hours ago. Which of the following should now be started specifically for fetal neuroprotection?
questions.explanation: Magnesium sulphate is given for fetal neuroprotection, as a 4 g bolus followed by a 1 g/h infusion for at least 4 hours, when imminent delivery is expected before 33+6 weeks gestation. It reduces the risk of cerebral palsy. This patient is at 30+2 weeks with advanced cervical dilatation and imminent delivery, so she meets the criteria.

optionExplanations.b: Nifedipine is a tocolytic used to delay delivery; tocolysis requires cervical dilatation under 4 cm and does not provide neuroprotection.
optionExplanations.c: Indomethacin is a tocolytic used in early preterm labour or polyhydramnios and has no neuroprotective role.
optionExplanations.d: Dexamethasone is an alternative antenatal corticosteroid for fetal lung maturity; she has already begun corticosteroid therapy with betamethasone.
optionExplanations.e: Antibiotics are given for group B Streptococcus prophylaxis, not for neuroprotection.

source.reference: OB18 — Preterm Labour Management: Neuroprotection

questions.question: A 25-year-old G1 at 33 weeks gestation presents after a sudden gush of clear fluid from the vagina, followed by continued leakage that has soaked through two pads. She has no contractions, bleeding, or fever, and the fetal heart rate is 145 bpm. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm rupture of membranes?

options.text: Transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length

questions.explanation: Prelabour rupture of membranes is confirmed by sterile speculum examination, which allows assessment for pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix, cascading of fluid from the cervix with cough or Valsalva, nitrazine testing, and ferning on microscopy. A sterile technique is used specifically to avoid introducing infection.

optionExplanations.a: Repeated or unnecessary digital examinations should be avoided because they increase the risk of infection and do not confirm membrane rupture.
optionExplanations.c: Cervical length measurement predicts preterm birth risk but does not establish whether membranes have ruptured.
optionExplanations.d: Fetal fibronectin testing requires intact membranes and is used to predict preterm labour, not to diagnose rupture.
optionExplanations.e: Amniocentesis is an invasive diagnostic procedure and has no role in confirming rupture of membranes.

source.reference: OB18 — Prelabour Rupture of Membranes: Investigations

questions.question: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 37 weeks gestation is found on ultrasound to have a frank breech presentation. The pregnancy is a singleton and has been uncomplicated, the membranes are intact, the presenting part is unengaged, the placenta is fundal, and the non-stress test is normal. She has no contraindication to vaginal delivery. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Schedule an elective caesarean delivery at 39 weeks
Await spontaneous version and reassess at 40 weeks
Induce labour for a planned vaginal breech delivery

questions.explanation: External cephalic version applies external pressure on the uterus to turn a non-vertex fetus to vertex, with an overall success rate of about 40-60%. The criteria are gestational age beyond 36 weeks, a singleton pregnancy, an unengaged presenting part, a reactive non-stress test, and intact membranes, all of which this patient meets. Both external cephalic version and elective caesarean delivery should be presented as options with informed consent.

optionExplanations.b: Elective caesarean delivery is a reasonable option but should only follow discussion of external cephalic version, which may avoid operative delivery entirely.
optionExplanations.c: There is no indication for urgent operative delivery in a stable, uncomplicated breech pregnancy at 37 weeks.
optionExplanations.d: Simply waiting forgoes the opportunity for version while the criteria are still met and the presenting part is unengaged.
optionExplanations.e: Induction for vaginal breech delivery is not the recommended next step when version has not yet been offered.

questions.topic: Fetal Malpresentation and External Cephalic Version

source.reference: OB25 — Breech Presentation: Management (ECV)

questions.question: A 33-year-old G1 at 35 weeks gestation presents with a persistent frontal headache. Her blood pressure is 168/114 mmHg on two seated readings 15 minutes apart, and her urine protein:creatinine ratio is 62 mg/mmol. Platelets, liver enzymes, and creatinine are normal, and the fetal heart tracing is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial antihypertensive?
questions.explanation: This patient has preeclampsia with severe hypertension, defined as a blood pressure above 160/110 mmHg. Initial therapy for severe hypertension should be labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa, or hydralazine, with the labetalol regimen being 20 mg IV followed by 20-80 mg IV every 30 minutes to a maximum of 300 mg before switching to oral therapy. Magnesium sulphate is given separately for seizure prophylaxis.

optionExplanations.b: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy and cause fetal renal defects, IUGR, and oligohydramnios.
optionExplanations.c: Atenolol is specifically listed among the agents that should not be used in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
optionExplanations.d: Diuretics are avoided except in the setting of pulmonary edema or cardiac failure, neither of which is present.
optionExplanations.e: Prazosin is among the agents that should not be used for hypertension in pregnancy.

source.reference: OB27 — Management of Hypertension and Preeclampsia

questions.question: A 31-year-old G2P1 at 26 weeks gestation undergoes routine screening for gestational diabetes using the preferred two-step approach, beginning with a random non-fasting 50 g oral glucose challenge test. Her 1-hour plasma glucose is 8.6 mmol/L. She is asymptomatic, her blood pressure is normal, and fetal growth is appropriate on ultrasound. Which of the following is the next best step?

options.text: Reassure her that screening is normal
Diagnose gestational diabetes and start insulin
Perform a fasting 75 g oral glucose tolerance test
Repeat the 50 g oral glucose challenge test in four weeks
Begin dietary modification and recheck fasting plasma glucose in two weeks

questions.explanation: In the preferred two-step screening strategy, a 1-hour plasma glucose below 7.8 mmol/L after the 50 g challenge is normal and a value of 11.1 mmol/L or more is diagnostic of gestational diabetes. An intermediate value of 7.8-11.0 mmol/L, as here, requires proceeding to step 2, a fasting 75 g oral glucose tolerance test.

optionExplanations.a: Values are only normal below 7.8 mmol/L; her result falls in the intermediate range requiring further testing.
optionExplanations.b: A diagnosis on the challenge test alone requires a 1-hour value of at least 11.1 mmol/L, and first-line treatment is diet and activity rather than immediate insulin.
optionExplanations.d: Repeating the screening test delays diagnosis; the intermediate result mandates confirmatory testing now.
optionExplanations.e: Treatment should not be started before the diagnosis is confirmed with the second-step test.

source.reference: OB29 — Gestational DM: Screening and Diagnosis

questions.question: A 29-year-old G1 at 39 weeks gestation is admitted in active labour. Her vaginal and anorectal culture at 36 weeks was positive for group B Streptococcus. She describes a previous reaction to penicillin with facial swelling and difficulty breathing requiring emergency treatment. Susceptibility testing of her isolate is not available. Which of the following is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Penicillin G 5 million units IV, then 2.5 million units IV every 4 hours
Cefazolin 2 g IV, then 1 g every 8 hours

questions.explanation: For group B Streptococcus prophylaxis in a patient with penicillin allergy who is at risk of anaphylaxis, vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours or clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours is used, but clindamycin only if the isolate is known to be susceptible. Since susceptibility is unknown here, vancomycin is appropriate. Antibiotics should be given at least 4 hours before delivery to be considered adequate.

optionExplanations.a: Penicillin G is first-line but is contraindicated given her history of anaphylaxis.
optionExplanations.b: Cefazolin is reserved for penicillin allergy with low risk of anaphylaxis, which does not apply to this patient.
optionExplanations.c: Clindamycin may only be used when the isolate is known to be susceptible, and susceptibility results are unavailable.
optionExplanations.e: Erythromycin is not among the recommended agents for intrapartum group B Streptococcus prophylaxis.

source.reference: OB30 — Early-Onset Group B Streptococcus Disease: Treatment

questions.question: A 28-year-old G1 at 40 weeks gestation is in active labour with oxytocin augmentation. Continuous cardiotocography shows repetitive uniform decelerations in which the onset, nadir, and recovery each occur after the peak of the contraction, with a slow return to baseline and a decrease in variability. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this pattern?

options.text: Fetal head compression with a vagal response

questions.explanation: Late decelerations are uniform in shape with onset, nadir, and recovery occurring after the peak of the contraction and a slow return to baseline, and they may cause decreased variability and a change in the baseline fetal heart rate. They reflect fetal hypoxia and acidemia, maternal hypotension, or uterine hypertonus, and are usually a sign of uteroplacental insufficiency.

optionExplanations.a: Cord compression causes variable decelerations, which vary in shape, onset, and duration with an abrupt drop in fetal heart rate.
optionExplanations.b: Head compression causes benign early decelerations that mirror the contraction, with the nadir at the peak of the contraction.
optionExplanations.d: Maternal fever produces fetal tachycardia rather than repetitive late decelerations.
optionExplanations.e: Fetal anemia is associated with a sinusoidal pattern and reduced oxygen carrying capacity, not with this deceleration pattern.

source.reference: OB37 — Table 18: Comparison of Decelerations

questions.question: A 33-year-old G2P1 with a pre-pregnancy BMI of 34 is delivering at 40 weeks gestation. After delivery of the fetal head, the head retracts tightly back against the perineum and the anterior shoulder fails to deliver with routine gentle downward traction. Additional help has been called to the room. Which of the following is the next best step?

options.text: Sharp fundal pressure during the next maternal push
Zavanelli manoeuvre with emergent caesarean delivery
Deliberate fracture of the neonatal clavicle

questions.explanation: The turtle sign, in which the delivered head retracts against the perineum, indicates shoulder dystocia. The goal is to displace the anterior shoulder from behind the symphysis pubis using a stepwise sequence of manoeuvres. After calling for help, the next steps are placing the legs in full flexion (McRoberts manoeuvre) and applying suprapubic pressure, which together resolve about 90% of cases.

optionExplanations.a: Fundal pressure is not part of the stepwise approach and worsens impaction of the anterior shoulder.
optionExplanations.c: The Zavanelli manoeuvre, replacing the fetus into the uterus for emergent caesarean delivery, is a last-line option.
optionExplanations.d: Cleidotomy is a last-line option after the standard stepwise manoeuvres have failed.
optionExplanations.e: Symphysiotomy is a last-line option reserved for failure of all standard manoeuvres.

source.reference: OB41 — Shoulder Dystocia: Presentation and Treatment

questions.question: A 30-year-old G4P4 has a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 40 weeks after a prolonged labour augmented with oxytocin. Within 20 minutes of delivery she loses approximately 800 mL of blood. The placenta was delivered intact with all membranes present, inspection of the cervix and vagina shows no lacerations, and the uterine fundus is soft and boggy above the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Postpartum hemorrhage is blood loss over 500 mL after vaginal delivery, and the causes are grouped as the 4 Ts: tone, tissue, trauma, and thrombin. Uterine atony is the most common cause, accounting for more than 80% of cases, and is suggested here by a soft, boggy, poorly contracted fundus. Risk factors present in this case include grand multiparity, prolonged labour, and oxytocin use causing uterine muscle exhaustion.

optionExplanations.b: Retained tissue is unlikely when the placenta and membranes were delivered intact.
optionExplanations.c: Trauma from a laceration has been excluded by inspection of the cervix and vagina, and would not produce a boggy uterus.
optionExplanations.d: Coagulopathy is usually identified before delivery and would not typically present with an atonic fundus in an otherwise healthy patient.
optionExplanations.e: Uterine inversion presents with an absent fundus on abdominal palpation and often a mass at the introitus, not a boggy fundus above the umbilicus.

source.reference: OB46 — Postpartum Hemorrhage: Etiology (4 Ts)

questions.question: A 30-year-old G2P1 at 30 weeks gestation is reviewed in the antenatal clinic. Prenatal serology shows she is rubella non-immune. She feels well, has had no rash or fever, and has already received her influenza vaccine and Tdap this pregnancy. She asks to be immunized against rubella now so that this and future pregnancies are protected. What is the most appropriate next step regarding rubella immunization?

options.text: Administer the measles/mumps/rubella vaccine at this visit
Administer the measles/mumps/rubella vaccine in the postpartum period
Administer immunoglobulin now and give the measles/mumps/rubella vaccine at 36 weeks gestation
Repeat rubella serology at 36 weeks and vaccinate antenatally if she remains non-immune
Defer any vaccination until 1 month after delivery and advise contraception during that interval

questions.explanation: Live vaccines, including measles/mumps/rubella, are avoided during pregnancy because of the risk of placental and fetal infection. Toronto Notes recommends the rubella vaccine postpartum for all non-immune patients, with pregnancy deferred for at least 1 month following vaccination. Influenza vaccine and Tdap are safe antenatally and she has already received both.

optionExplanations.a: Measles/mumps/rubella is a live attenuated vaccine and is avoided in pregnancy because of the risk of placental and fetal infection.
optionExplanations.c: Immunoglobulin has no role here, and giving a live vaccine at 36 weeks is still antenatal administration; in fact receipt of immunoglobulin or blood products is a reason to delay postpartum vaccination.
optionExplanations.d: Repeating serology does not change the rule that live vaccines are avoided during pregnancy; non-immune status has already been established.
optionExplanations.e: The 1 month deferral applies to becoming pregnant after vaccination, not to delaying the vaccine itself; any vaccine required is generally safe postpartum and should be given before discharge.

source.reference: OB13 — Immunizations: Intrapartum and Postpartum

questions.question: A 32-year-old G1 with chronic hypertension is seen at 34 weeks gestation. Growth was normal at her 20-week anatomy scan. Ultrasound now shows an estimated fetal weight below the 10th percentile. The fetal abdomen is disproportionately smaller than the fetal head, and the head circumference to abdominal circumference ratio is increased. There are no structural anomalies and TORCH serology is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Symmetric (type I) intrauterine growth restriction secondary to a TORCH infection
Symmetric (type I) intrauterine growth restriction secondary to a chromosomal abnormality
Symmetric (type I) intrauterine growth restriction secondary to maternal malnutrition
Asymmetric (type II) intrauterine growth restriction secondary to placental insufficiency

questions.explanation: Asymmetric/type II IUGR accounts for about 70% of cases and occurs late in pregnancy: the fetal abdomen is disproportionately smaller than the fetal head because the brain is spared, so the HC/AC ratio is increased. It is usually associated with placental insufficiency, and chronic HTN is a listed maternal risk factor. Prognosis is more favourable than type I.

optionExplanations.a: Symmetric/type I IUGR occurs early in pregnancy with reduced growth of both head and abdomen; TORCH serology is negative and growth was normal at 20 weeks.
optionExplanations.b: Congenital anomalies and chromosomal abnormalities cause the early, symmetric pattern with proportionate head and abdominal growth, not the asymmetric pattern described.
optionExplanations.c: Maternal malnutrition is a recognized risk factor for IUGR, but the disproportionate abdominal lag with brain sparing points to placental insufficiency rather than a symmetric type I pattern.
optionExplanations.e: Intrauterine fetal demise requires absent cardiac activity and fetal movement on ultrasound; growth restriction alone does not establish it.

source.reference: OB20 — Intrauterine Growth Restriction: Clinical Features

questions.question: A 31-year-old G1 at 33 weeks gestation has a twin pregnancy. Ultrasound at 10 weeks gestation determined chorionicity as monochorionic monoamniotic. Serial scans every 2 weeks since 16 weeks show concordant growth with a discrepancy under 25%, both twins are cephalic, and biophysical profiles are reassuring. She wants to know how her twins should be delivered. What is the most appropriate plan for mode of delivery?

options.text: Attempt vaginal delivery because twin A presents as vertex
Attempt vaginal delivery because the growth discrepancy is less than 25%
Attempt vaginal delivery of twin A, with caesarean delivery of twin B
Attempt vaginal delivery with external cephalic version of twin B if it changes presentation

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that all monochorionic monoamniotic twins need to be delivered by caesarean delivery, largely because of the risk of twin interlocking and cord entanglement in MCMA twins. The option of attempting vaginal delivery when twin A is vertex with a growth discrepancy under 25% applies to dichorionic diamniotic or monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies, not monoamniotic ones.

optionExplanations.b: A vertex presenting twin A permits a trial of vaginal delivery only in dichorionic diamniotic or monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies; monoamniotic twins are excluded.
optionExplanations.c: A growth discrepancy under 25% is one criterion for attempting vaginal delivery in diamniotic twins, but it does not override the requirement for caesarean delivery in monoamniotic twins.
optionExplanations.d: Combined vaginal then caesarean delivery describes an unplanned outcome in roughly 10% of twin deliveries, not a planned approach for monoamniotic twins.
optionExplanations.e: Mode of delivery in twins depends on chorionicity, fetal weights, gestational age and presentation; planned caesarean is required here regardless of presentation changes.

source.reference: OB23 — Multi-Fetal Gestation and Fetal Malpresentation: Management

questions.question: A 26-year-old G1 at 39 weeks gestation has been in labour for 18 hours after rupture of membranes 26 hours earlier, with multiple vaginal exams. Her temperature is 39.0°C and she is tachycardic. The uterus is tender and the cervical discharge is foul and purulent. The cervix is 7 cm dilated with the head at 0 station. The fetal heart rate baseline is 180 bpm. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: IV ampicillin and gentamicin with clindamycin for anaerobic coverage, allowing labour to progress
Antipyretics alone while awaiting spontaneous delivery
Withhold antibiotics until the amniotic fluid Gram stain and culture results return
Clindamycin given postpartum only, and only if caesarean delivery becomes necessary

questions.explanation: Maternal fever of 39.0°C with fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and foul purulent cervical discharge after prolonged rupture of membranes and multiple vaginal exams is diagnostic of chorioamnionitis. Treatment is IV ampicillin 2 g q6h plus gentamicin, with anaerobic coverage such as clindamycin, together with antipyretics. Chorioamnionitis is not an indication for immediate delivery or caesarean delivery, so proper labour progression is allowed.

optionExplanations.a: Chorioamnionitis itself is not an indication for immediate delivery or caesarean delivery, especially if delivery is imminent and can be done safely.
optionExplanations.c: Antipyretics are adjunctive; without IV antibiotics she is at risk of bacteremia, pelvic abscess, wound infection and maternal or neonatal sepsis.
optionExplanations.d: Amniotic fluid Gram stain, glucose and culture support the diagnosis but treatment should not be delayed for results.
optionExplanations.e: Antibiotics are needed now; postpartum continuation is considered for those at risk of endometritis, especially after caesarean delivery, and is not a substitute for intrapartum treatment.

source.reference: OB43 — Chorioamnionitis: Clinical Features and Treatment

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman who delivered vaginally 3 weeks ago presents with 2 days of unilateral localized breast pain. The affected breast has an area of erythema and marked tenderness. There is no fluctuant mass, no subareolar mass, and no purulent nipple discharge. Her temperature is 38.4°C. She has no drug allergies, does not smoke, and wishes to continue breastfeeding. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Cloxacillin with continued nursing and pumping, plus heat or ice packs
Discontinue nursing and start IV nafcillin with incision and drainage
Broad-spectrum antibiotics with incision and drainage
Fine-needle aspiration of the affected area to exclude cancer

questions.explanation: Lactational mastitis typically occurs 2-3 weeks postpartum, is caused by S. aureus, and presents with unilateral localized pain, tenderness and erythema. Treatment is heat or ice packs, continued nursing or pumping, and antibiotics such as cloxacillin or cephalexin (erythromycin if penicillin-allergic). She has no fluctuant mass or purulent nipple discharge, so an abscess is not present.

optionExplanations.b: Discontinuing nursing with IV nafcillin or oxacillin and incision and drainage is reserved for a lactational breast abscess, indicated by a fluctuant mass, purulent nipple discharge, fever and leukocytosis.
optionExplanations.c: Broad-spectrum antibiotics with incision and drainage is the treatment for non-lactational mastitis, which typically presents with subareolar pain and nipple inversion around a mean age of 32 years.
optionExplanations.d: Fine-needle aspiration to exclude cancer is used when a non-lactational mass does not resolve, not for a classic lactational presentation 3 weeks postpartum.
optionExplanations.e: Total duct excision is the definitive treatment for recurrent periductal (non-lactational) mastitis, not for acute lactational mastitis.

source.reference: OB49 — Table 22: Lactational vs. Non-Lactational Mastitis

questions.question: A 32-year-old G3P2 at 30 weeks gestation presents with a second episode of bright red vaginal bleeding that began while she was resting and has now stopped on its own. She reports no abdominal pain and no contractions. Her uterus is soft and non-tender, the presenting fetal part is high, and the fetal heart rate is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Placenta previa is a placenta implanted in the lower segment of the uterus covering the internal cervical os, and it causes painless bright red vaginal bleeding that is recurrent and may cease spontaneously, with a mean onset of bleeding at 30 wk GA. On examination the uterus is soft and non-tender, the presenting fetal part is high or displaced, and the FHR is usually normal, which is exactly this presentation. In contrast, bleeding from placental abruption is usually painful. Do not perform a digital vaginal exam until placenta previa has been ruled out by U/S; speculum and transvaginal probe are safe.

optionExplanations.a: Bloody show represents cervical changes and early dilation and is the most common physiologic etiology of third-trimester bleeding, but she has no contractions and the bleeding is recurrent and frankly bright red.
optionExplanations.c: Abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and bleeding is usually painful, with risk factors such as maternal hypertension, smoking, cocaine, or trauma; her uterus is soft and non-tender.
optionExplanations.d: Vasa previa is in the differential for antepartum hemorrhage but characteristically bleeds at rupture of membranes; her membranes are intact and the bleeding is recurrent and painless.
optionExplanations.e: Uterine rupture is listed in the differential diagnosis of antepartum hemorrhage but is not suggested here without labour, pain, or a previous uterine scar.

source.reference: OB14 — Antepartum Hemorrhage: Placenta Previa

questions.question: A 27-year-old G1 has a vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery at 40 weeks gestation after a second stage lasting three hours. Inspection of the perineal laceration shows a tear that involves the fascia and muscles of the perineal body and extends through the external anal sphincter and the internal anal sphincter. The rectal mucosa is intact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A 3rd degree laceration involves the anal sphincter and is subdivided as 3A (<50% of external anal sphincter), 3B (>50% of external anal sphincter), and 3C (external and internal anal sphincters). A 4th degree laceration extends through the anal sphincter complex (external and internal) and into the rectal mucosa. This patient's external and internal anal sphincters are both involved while the rectal mucosa is spared, so this is a 3C injury; vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery and a second stage of labour longer than 2 h are risk factors for obstetric anal sphincter injuries.

optionExplanations.a: A 2nd degree laceration involves the fascia and muscles of the perineal body but not the anal sphincter, which is involved in this patient.
optionExplanations.b: 3A is a tear of <50% of the external anal sphincter, whereas her external anal sphincter is disrupted along its full thickness.
optionExplanations.c: 3B is >50% of the external anal sphincter without involvement of the internal anal sphincter, which is also involved here.
optionExplanations.e: A 4th degree laceration extends through the anal sphincter complex and into the rectal mucosa, which is intact on examination.

source.reference: OB44 — Perineal Lacerations

questions.question: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 15 weeks gestation attends a routine prenatal visit. She feels well, with no dysuria, urgency, or frequency, and no fever, flank pain, or costovertebral angle tenderness. A routine urinalysis and urine culture grow Escherichia coli. This is her first positive culture of the pregnancy. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 250-500 mg q8h for 7 d, then monthly urine cultures
No antibiotics; repeat the urine culture only if dysuria, urgency, or frequency develops
Continuous nitrofurantoin prophylaxis for the remainder of the pregnancy, without a treatment course
Renal function tests, with antibiotics withheld pending the results

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that asymptomatic bacteriuria should be treated in pregnancy because of the increased risk of progression to cystitis and pyelonephritis and a probable increased risk of PTL. For uncomplicated UTI the first-line agent is amoxicillin 250-500 mg PO q8h for 7 d, with nitrofurantoin or cephalosporins as alternatives, followed by monthly urine cultures. This patient has a positive screening culture with no fever, flank pain, or costovertebral angle tenderness to suggest pyelonephritis, so an oral first-line course with monthly culture follow-up is appropriate.

optionExplanations.b: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated rather than observed in pregnancy, precisely because of the increased risk of pyelonephritis and PTL.
optionExplanations.c: Hospitalization and IV antibiotics are reserved for pyelonephritis, which presents with fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness.
optionExplanations.d: Continuous or post-coital prophylaxis is offered when recurrence occurs, not instead of treating a first positive culture, and it is avoided in the last 4 wk of pregnancy.
optionExplanations.e: Renal function tests are indicated in recurrent infections; they do not substitute for prompt treatment of bacteriuria.

source.reference: OB31 — Urinary Tract Infection

questions.question: A 29-year-old G2P1 at 32 weeks gestation is seen because her uterus measures small for dates. She reports no leakage of fluid and normal fetal movement. Ultrasound shows a single deepest pocket of 1.5 cm and an amniotic fluid index of 4 cm, with no fetal anomaly identified. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure her and repeat the ultrasound in 4 wk, as no treatment is required
Admission for investigation, ruling out ROM, with fetal monitoring by NST and BPP
Therapeutic amniocentesis to decompress the uterus

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines oligohydramnios as an AFI <5 cm or a single deepest pocket <2 cm and states that it warrants admission and investigation: rule out ROM, fetal monitoring with NST and BPP, U/S Doppler studies of the umbilical cord and uterine artery, and maternal hydration, with delivery considered if term. This patient's AFI of 4 cm and single deepest pocket of 1.5 cm meet that definition, and because oligohydramnios marks an infant who may not tolerate labour well, she needs admission and fetal surveillance rather than outpatient follow-up. At 32 wk GA she is not term, so investigation precedes any decision about delivery.

optionExplanations.a: Observation without treatment applies to mild to moderate polyhydramnios; oligohydramnios warrants admission and investigation.
optionExplanations.c: Therapeutic amniocentesis is reserved for severe polyhydramnios with an overdistended uterus, and would further reduce an already low fluid volume.
optionExplanations.d: Amnio-infusion via an intrauterine catheter is considered during labour, not as the initial step in an undelivered patient at 32 wk GA.
optionExplanations.e: Delivery is considered if the pregnancy is at term; at 32 wk GA the priority is investigation and fetal monitoring.

source.reference: OB22 — Polyhydramnios/Oligohydramnios
